subtype: Worry showing as stomach aches and clinging [Actor]
passage: Every morning before the school bus, Charu said her tummy hurt. At the stop in their small town, she clung to her father's leg and cried. "What if the bus doesn't bring me back? What if you're not here?" Hemant knelt. He didn't say, "Don't be silly." He said, "Your tummy feels the worry. That's real." They made a routine: same rhyme on the walk, same wave at the neem tree. The first day, he rode the bus with her. The next week, he waved from the stop and stood right there when the bus came back. By the end of the month, Charu let go at the neem tree herself.

qa.q: Where did Charu and Hemant wave every morning?
Why did Charu's tummy hurt before the bus?
qa.a: She was frightened, worrying that the bus wouldn't bring her back or that her father wouldn't be there.

qa.q: What small steps helped Charu most?
qa.a: A calm, fixed routine and gradual steps: riding the bus with her first, then waving from the stop and always being there when she returned.

qa.q: What would change if Hemant had said, 'Don't be silly'?
qa.a: Charu might feel her worry wasn't believed and cling harder, since her fear would feel even more alone.

grounding: It shows a young child with tummy aches and clinging before school and many what-if questions, helped by a calm routine and gentle steps toward the bus.

subtype: Worry showing as stomach aches and clinging [Actor]
passage: At the pool in Helsinki, Valentina sat on the bench in her swimsuit, holding her stomach. "Papa, my tummy hurts. What if the water goes in my nose? What if I sink?" Sami sat down beside her. "Worry can make your tummy hurt. Let's go slowly. Today, we just watch." They watched the other children splash. The next Saturday, Valentina sat on the edge and put her toes in. "It's cold!" she squeaked. The next, she stood in the shallow end, holding Sami's hand, while the teacher showed her how to blow bubbles. In the changing room afterwards, she said, "My tummy didn't hurt today, Papa."

qa.q: What did Valentina and Sami do at the pool on the first day?
qa.a: They just watched the other children splash.

qa.q: What was Valentina worried about at the pool?
qa.a: She was worried water would go in her nose and that she would sink.

qa.q: Which approach did Sami choose, and why did it work?
qa.a: He went slowly, one small step each week, from watching to toes to standing in the shallow end, so her fear shrank.

qa.q: How might the swimming teacher see Valentina's progress?
qa.a: The teacher might see a child growing braver week by week, ready to learn bubbles once she felt safe.

grounding: It shows a young child with a tummy ache and what-if questions before swimming, and a father who uses calm, gentle steps toward the feared water.
